name: Tábor Gate (Táborská brána)
historical description: The southern outer gate belongs to the Baroque fortress built in the mid-17th century. Earlier, the road from Prague toward South Bohemia passed through a busy settlement whose market space extended toward the site of the later Leopold Gate. By the late 19th century, arrivals passed a military guard and crossed the fortress moat before reaching the food-tax office, horse-watering pump and city guards near the remains of Špička.

name: Špička Gate (Špička)
historical description: Built in 1348–1350 under Charles IV, Špička was a Gothic gate with two towers linked by a walkway and nine pointed spires. A drawbridge crossed a moat cut into the rock. After the Tábor Gate extended the defences, Špička became a military storehouse and was gradually reduced to the surviving ground floor of its northern tower. Look for the two former portal arches, the portcullis groove and the ring used to fasten a closing chain; the masonry also preserves marks associated with guards sharpening their swords.

name: Gothic wall fragments near Špička
historical description: Remains of Vyšehrad’s medieval defensive masonry, incorporated into or exposed beside later fortifications. The masonry is evidence of successive defensive phases: older medieval structures were often absorbed, altered, or hidden by the later fortress. Looking closely at changes in stonework can reveal that the site was rebuilt rather than created in one moment.

name: Leopold Gate (Leopoldova brána)
historical description: A monumental Baroque fortress gate built in the late 17th century and named for Emperor Leopold I. Its position is best understood as part of a sequence of controlled entrances: visitors and troops passed through successive barriers rather than a single open doorway. The surviving structure therefore helps explain how the fortress regulated movement as well as defended itself.

name: Brick Gate (Cihelná brána)
historical description: An Empire-style gate dating from 1841. It later became an important entrance to the fortress’s casemate system. Its position is best understood as part of a sequence of controlled entrances: visitors and troops passed through successive barriers rather than a single open doorway. The surviving structure therefore helps explain how the fortress regulated movement as well as defended itself.

name: Vyšehrad fortress walls
historical description: The extensive walls that transformed Vyšehrad into a Baroque military fortress, largely during the 17th and 18th centuries. The masonry is evidence of successive defensive phases: older medieval structures were often absorbed, altered, or hidden by the later fortress. Looking closely at changes in stonework can reveal that the site was rebuilt rather than created in one moment.

name: Baroque bastions
historical description: Angular defensive platforms built to protect the fortress from artillery attack. Bastions were designed for the age of artillery, allowing defenders to cover the faces of neighbouring walls and reduce blind spots. Their geometry is a key clue to reading Vyšehrad as an engineered fortress rather than simply a medieval castle.

historical description: A surviving medieval cellar associated with Vyšehrad’s former royal and residential buildings. name: Royal Palace (Královský palác)
historical description: The fortified royal precinct combined palaces with a large courtyard. Charles IV commissioned four palaces on the site of the earlier, 11th-century residence. The former burgrave’s office survives, while low masonry near the later gunpowder store records the assembly palace and its upper-floor feasting hall. A cellar from the residential palace was adapted for ammunition storage in 1653 and now houses an exhibition. The low remains shown here should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the lost buildings.

name: Royal courtyard
historical description: The area of the former medieval royal precinct, now largely altered by later construction and fortification. This feature belongs to the period when Vyšehrad was a royal and ecclesiastical centre, not merely a fortress. It helps reconstruct the settlement that preceded the Baroque military enclosure.

name: Church of the Decollation of St. John the Baptist
historical description: This Gothic church survives, partly incorporated into the fortress rampart behind the Chapel of Our Lady of the Ramparts. Dating to at least the later 14th century, it served the local parish and cemetery between the 15th and 17th centuries. Fortress construction removed part of the building, but it was not completely destroyed. After a period of military use, the Vyšehrad Chapter bought and restored it in 1882. The real interior is accessible on guided tours; this model represents its exposed exterior, not a surveyed interior.

name: Memorial to the lost Church of St. John the Baptist
historical description: The nearby interpretation board explains a hidden, surviving church, rather than a completely lost one. St. John the Baptist was partly demolished and absorbed into the Baroque rampart. Its remaining structure stands behind the later Ave Maria chapel and was restored after the Vyšehrad Chapter acquired it in 1882. Its concealed position is a particularly clear example of medieval religious architecture being reused by the fortress.

name: Chapel of Our Lady of the Ramparts
historical description: A small chapel associated with the later religious landscape of the fortress and the area of earlier medieval structures. The chapel illustrates how devotional life continued within a precinct repeatedly reshaped by military needs. Its location is as important as its architecture, since religious buildings were woven into the fortress’s everyday landscape.

historical description: Archaeological remains of an early Romanesque church, evidence of Vyšehrad’s religious importance before the Gothic period. This feature belongs to the period when Vyšehrad was a royal and ecclesiastical centre, not merely a fortress. It helps reconstruct the settlement that preceded the Baroque military enclosure.

name: Early church foundations
historical description: Archaeological foundations showing that Vyšehrad’s religious history reaches back to the early medieval period. The building or remains reflect Vyšehrad’s role as a religious centre as well as a strategic stronghold. Its history should be read alongside the nearby chapter buildings and the changing patronage of Bohemian rulers and clergy.

name: Romanesque bridge remains
historical description: Built around 1070, this single-arch stone bridge crossed the moat of the Royal Acropolis. It was about 22 metres long and connected with a covered stone passage leading towards the earlier basilica, probably providing a ceremonial entrance for the ruler. It is the oldest known stone-bridge construction in the Czech Republic. The bridge and moat disappeared before the 13th century, and archaeologists uncovered the surviving masonry in 1935. Only the archaeological remains, not the complete medieval bridge, are represented here.

name: Medieval defensive wall
historical description: Surviving sections of Vyšehrad’s earlier medieval fortifications, predating the Baroque fortress. historical description: A medieval tower ruin on the Vyšehrad rock. Its name is rooted in legend; it was a defensive structure, not a bath. The work translates historical or legendary narratives into public art. Its placement in Vyšehrad is significant because the fortress became a powerful setting for stories about the origins and destiny of the Czech nation.

name: Basilica of Sts. Peter and Paul

The building or remains reflect Vyšehrad’s role as a religious centre as well as a strategic stronghold. name: Rotunda of St. Martin
historical description: St. Martin’s Rotunda was built around 1100, outside the Royal Acropolis, and is one of Prague’s oldest surviving churches. It later served as a prison and gunpowder store, was reconsecrated in 1719, and returned to military use in 1784. Karel Chotek helped save it when a new road threatened the building. The Vyšehrad Chapter bought it in 1875 and restored it, adding the present Neo-Romanesque entrance. The blocked earlier doorway remains visible above the road, and the cannonball recalls the Prussian siege of 1757.

The model follows that surviving form rather than restoring the lost canopy. The nearby equestrian St. Wenceslas is a copy of the Baroque statue Štulc rescued from Wenceslas Square.

name: Popelka Biliánová’s House
historical description: House no. 12 combined the food-tax office with the tax collector's family home. Traders waited nearby with their carts and watered their horses at the pump; charges depended on the food being brought into Prague. The collector married the writer Popelka Biliánová in 1892. Her collecting and retelling of local legends made this modest roadside house part of Vyšehrad's literary history.

name: Jedlička Institute
historical description: Founded in 1913 through the work of Rudolf Jedlička and his collaborators, the institute developed education, practical workshops and rehabilitation for children and young people with physical disabilities. Its early Vyšehrad premises included house no. 13, a former inn and military lodging nicknamed 'Poland' after a brief stay by Polish soldiers. The institute continues its educational and rehabilitation work today.
